cultural_notes: Woccon is a Native American tribal name with multiple historical spellings
Documented from early 16th to late 18th century European sources
Variations include Guacaya (1521), Wococon (1606), Wokakon (1607), Wacawn (1699)
Also known as 'Northward's Indians' and 'Parched Corn Indians'
Documented in maps, colonial records, and historical texts
Spelling variations suggest complex linguistic documentation and transcription challenges
Woccon belonged to the Siouan linguistic stock
Closest linguistic relations were the Catawba
Primarily lived between Neuse River and its affluents, near present-day Goldsboro, Wayne County, North Carolina
First documented by Lawson around 1701, who recorded 150 words of their language
Estimated population of 600 in 1600, with 120 warriors in 1701
Participated in Tuscarora Wars (1711-1715)
Likely extinguished as a tribe during Tuscarora Wars
Remnants potentially fled north with Tuscarora, united with Catawba, or combined with other Siouan groups
Only southern eastern Siouan tribe besides Catawba with preserved vocabulary
Woccon/Waccamaw people historically lived along Waccamaw and Pee Dee Rivers in South/North Carolina
Experienced significant disruption from Spanish entrada in 16th-17th centuries
Shared ties with Cheraw/Saraw, Waccamaw of NC, Lumbee, Cape Fear, and Catawba tribes
Experienced repeated displacement and interactions with European explorers
By 1670, English documented their presence along Waccamaw and Pee Dee Rivers
Suffered from slave trade and inter-tribal conflicts
Some groups became 'Tribute Indians' to survive European pressures
Woccon identified as Siouan stock by John Lawson in 1701
Recorded 120 fighting men and two towns: Yupwareremau and Tooptatmeer
Total population around 500 inhabitants in 1701
Participated in Tuscarora War (1711-1713) alongside Barnwell's Army
Woccon name disappears around the same time Waccamaw name appears
Part of Capt. Bull's Company during Tuscarora War
Some tribal movement noted with a group breaking away from main settlement and relocating southward
Waccamaw were a Native American tribe located in South Carolina near the Pee Dee and Black Rivers
In 1715, they had approximately 610 people living between the Waccamaw and Pee Dee Rivers
They were often associated with the Cape Fear and Cheraw tribes
They participated in the Yamassee War in 1715, attacking South Carolina alongside other native nations
In 1718, they experienced a conflict known as the Waccamaw War, resulting in 60 killed or taken prisoner
By 1720, they were located approximately 100 miles northeast of Charleston
Historical documentation comes from sources like John Swanton (Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin, 1952), McDowell (1992), and Sainsbury (1928-1947)
Waccamaw were a Native American tribe operating independently near Catawba territory
Faced raids and enslavement by Seneca, Cherokee, and other groups
Sought refuge with Winyaw and Pedee in 1723
Lived primarily in North Carolina on Lumber River in 1725
Potentially incorporated with or absorbed by Catawba or English settlements
Documented by anthropologists like Mooney (1894), Hodge (1910), and Swanton (1952)
Experienced significant displacement and conflict with European settlers in early 18th century
Waccamaw people are a Siouan tribal group located in parts of South Carolina and North Carolina
By 1734, their traditional lands around Lake Waccamaw were largely depopulated
In 1778, many Waccamaw fled to North Carolina swamps for protection
The Dimery Settlement was a key community for Waccamaw-Siouan people in Robeson County, NC
Modern tribal recognition occurred in 1992 with an initial organizational meeting on October 17th
Historically documented as a 'small friendly tribe' by 1751
Experienced significant displacement and social marginalization through the 18th-20th centuries
Maintained community identity through church establishments, schools, and land ownership
Woccon was an Eastern Siouan language most closely related to Catawba
Woccon is considered a dormant language
Woccon was a subdivision of the Waccamaw people
Waccamaw territory extended from Winyah Bay up Waccamaw River to the Cape Fear, and somewhat to the Neuse River
Primary historical documentation sources include Adelung & Vater (1806), John Lawson (1709), and Blair A. Rudes (1985)
The Woccon language is part of the Eastern Siouan linguistic branch
The Waccamaw Siouan tribe received federal recognition in 2005
HR1942 was signed in 2021 related to tribal recognition
Woccon is a Siouan language from coastal North Carolina
Documented in scholarly sources like Rudes (2000) and Carter (1980)
Historical sources include Colonial Records of NC and journals from early 18th century
Studied in context of Native American linguistic and cultural research
Woccon is a Siouan language from the Carolinas
Documentation sources include Frank G. Speck's anthropological work in American Anthropologist (1935)
Historical documentation spans colonial records from 1650-1770
Scholarly sources include works by McDowell, Merrell, Rights, Sainsbury, and Salley
